Q2459887.summary: A Pharisee, coarse-featured and seen in shadowed profile, holds out a coin to test Christ, who turns with calm, luminous dignity and points to it. Titian sets the two heads in close contrast, the radiant, gentle face of Christ against the worldly questioner, illustrating the answer 'Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and unto God the things that are God's.'
facts: It was painted for Duke Alfonso I d'Este of Ferrara, reportedly as the door of a cabinet holding his collection of coins and medals.
Titian signed the work on the Pharisee's white collar, 'TICIANUS F.', making it his earliest signed painting.
Contemporaries such as Vasari praised the head of Christ as a marvel of painting.
